```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5)
```

A Bayesian network represents a joint distribution over variables
$X_1, \dots, X_n$ by a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and one conditional
distribution per node:
$$P(X_1, \dots, X_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n P(X_i \mid \mathrm{Pa}(X_i)).$$
The graph encodes conditional independencies (read off by d-separation) and,
under causal assumptions, the effects of interventions.

```{r}
library(pgmcompR)
```

## Building a network by hand

We model a simplified diagnostic problem. Smoking raises the risk of lung
cancer; cancer makes an abnormal chest X-ray and shortness of breath more
likely.

```{r}
bn <- bayesian_network(list(
  c("Smoking", "Cancer"),
  c("Cancer", "XRay"),
  c("Cancer", "Dyspnea")
))
bn
```

Conditional distributions are added node by node. A root node takes a named
probability vector. A node with parents takes a matrix whose rows are the
child's states and whose columns are parent configurations; the parents'
state labels come from the variable registry.

```{r}
bn <- add_cpd(bn, "Smoking", c(no = 0.7, yes = 0.3))
bn <- add_cpd(bn, "Cancer", matrix(c(0.995, 0.005,
                                     0.95,  0.05), nrow = 2,
                                   dimnames = list(c("no", "yes"), NULL)))
bn <- add_cpd(bn, "XRay", matrix(c(0.9, 0.1,
                                   0.2, 0.8), nrow = 2,
                                 dimnames = list(c("negative", "positive"), NULL)))
bn <- add_cpd(bn, "Dyspnea", matrix(c(0.85, 0.15,
                                      0.35, 0.65), nrow = 2,
                                    dimnames = list(c("no", "yes"), NULL)))
check_model(bn)
get_cpd(bn, "Cancer")
variable_registry(bn)
```

`check_model()` verifies that every node has a CPD, that parents match the
graph, that every column sums to one and that state labels agree across
CPDs. Mistakes are reported rather than repaired:

```{r, error = TRUE}
cpd("Smoking", c(no = 0.7, yes = 0.4))
```

## Queries

`query()` returns the posterior of the query variables as a normalized
factor. The default method is exact variable elimination.

```{r}
query(bn, "Cancer", evidence = list(XRay = "positive"))
query(bn, "Cancer", evidence = list(XRay = "positive", Dyspnea = "yes", Smoking = "yes"))
```

A joint query returns a factor over several variables; `joint = FALSE`
returns marginals instead.

```{r}
query(bn, c("Cancer", "Smoking"), evidence = list(XRay = "positive"))
```

The most probable explanation and maximum a posteriori assignments are
different queries from marginal posteriors:

```{r}
mpe_query(bn, evidence = list(XRay = "positive"))
map_query(bn, "Cancer", evidence = list(XRay = "positive"))
```

Here the posterior probability of cancer given a positive X-ray is still
small, so the MAP state of `Cancer` is `"no"`, even though the evidence
raised its probability more than tenfold.

## Independence and the Markov blanket

```{r}
d_separated(bn, "XRay", "Dyspnea", "Cancer")
d_separated(bn, "XRay", "Dyspnea")
markov_blanket(bn, "Cancer")
```

## Observation versus intervention

Observing a positive X-ray changes our belief about smoking; forcing the
X-ray machine to print "positive" does not:

```{r}
query(bn, "Smoking", evidence = list(XRay = "positive"))
do_query(bn, "Smoking", interventions = list(XRay = "positive"))
```

## Simulation

```{r}
set.seed(1)
d <- simulate_bn(bn, 5)
d
```

## Plotting

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(bn, evidence = "XRay")
```

## Example networks

The package ships classic networks for experimentation:
`example_network("asia")`, `"sprinkler"`, `"cancer"`, `"student"` and
`"gaussian"`. The remaining vignettes use them to cover learning, exact and
approximate inference, Markov networks, Gaussian and dynamic models, causal
queries, interoperability, extension and performance.
